passage: Divyansh, you want to know how I met my oldest friend, Hari? Sit, and your Binita Dida will tell you. When I was ten, in our small school in Siliguri, the boys used to push Hari against the wall and call him names. Everyone watched. I watched too, for a long time. One day my stomach just said enough. I went and sat next to him on the step, my knees shaking. "Come play with us," I said. He looked at me like I had grown wings. That evening, I went to Sen Sir and told him everything. He did not call me a tattletale. He listened, thanked me, and spoke to the class the next morning. After that, two more girls sat with us. Things changed.

passage:
At recess in the colony school in Pune, Jomon sat alone on the steps again. For two weeks, Vicky's group had told everyone not to play with him.

Chinmay watched from the football game. His stomach felt funny. Then he walked over and sat down next to Jomon.

"Come play with us," he said. "We need a goalkeeper."

Jomon looked at him, then at Vicky's group. "They'll get angry."

"Let them."

Jomon went. He was terrible in goal. Everyone laughed, but not at him. With him.

After recess Chinmay stopped at the staffroom and told Mrs Pillai what had been happening. He was nervous. She said, "Thank you. That's not tale-telling. That's brave." She spoke to Vicky's group the same afternoon.

The next day, two more boys asked Jomon to play.

qa.q: What position did Jomon play?
qa.a: Goalkeeper.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel before walking over to Jomon?
qa.a: His stomach felt funny; he felt nervous but decided to act anyway.

qa.a: Sitting beside Jomon and inviting him to play changed the group's mood, and telling Mrs Pillai got an adult to act the same day.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when two more boys ask him to play the next day?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and included, less alone than before.

grounding: Chinmay sits beside Jomon, invites him to play and tells a teacher, showing that standing with the target is brave and changes the group's mood.

"Harish, why are you sitting here alone again?"

"Irfan... they said nobody should talk to me."

"Who said?"

"Kunal's gang. Because I cried in PE."

"That's stupid. Come play kho-kho with us."

"They'll stop talking to you too."

"Let them. Come on."

Later, after the bell.

"Ma'am, can I tell you something?"

"Of course, Irfan."

"Kunal's gang has been telling everyone not to talk to Harish. For a week. He sits alone every day."

"Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing."

"It's not tale-telling?"

"No. Telling an adult when someone's being hurt is brave. I'll speak to them today, and I'll make sure Harish is okay."

passage:
I didn't plan to do anything brave. It just happened.

Divyansh had been sitting under the mango tree alone at lunch for days, ever since the boys started calling him "Chuha." Everyone knew. Nobody did anything.

That Tuesday I took my tiffin and sat next to him. My heart was going very fast. I said, "Come play hopscotch with us after lunch." He looked at me like I'd said something in Japanese. Then he came.

The next day, Priyal joined too. And then Anu. By Friday there were five of us, and the boys stopped shouting "Chuha" because nobody laughed anymore.

I also told our class teacher, Mr Kapoor, on Tuesday afternoon. I thought he'd say I was a tattletale. He said I was brave, and he talked to the boys that day.

— Hafsa

qa.q: What did the boys call Divyansh?
qa.a: "Chuha."

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel sitting down next to Divyansh?
qa.a: Hafsa felt nervous, heart going very fast, but went ahead anyway.

qa.q: How did Hafsa's actions change the group's mood?
qa.a: Sitting with Divyansh and inviting him to play drew other children in, so the teasing stopped getting laughs, and telling Mr Kapoor brought an adult in.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt when Hafsa invited him to play?
qa.a: He was surprised and probably relieved and grateful, no longer alone under the mango tree.

grounding: Hafsa sits beside Divyansh, invites him to play and tells a teacher, and her small act of standing with him changes the group's mood.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 4A, Friday. At lunch break I noticed Shalini sitting alone on the steps again, as she has most days since some Class 6 girls started calling her names. Today Urmila walked over, sat beside her and said, loud enough for others to hear, "Come play with us. We need one more for kho-kho." Shalini hesitated, then went. Within minutes two more girls had joined their game. After the bell Urmila came to my desk, twisting her plait. "Ma'am, I'm not telling tales, but the Class 6 girls are mean to Shalini every day." I told her this was not tale-telling; it was brave and right. I spoke gently with Shalini that afternoon and, before leaving, reported it to our safeguarding lead and to her parents.
